Forecasts may follow the coarse trend of the observed future, but fail to preserve sharp changes, oscillations, turning points, and regime transitions that define plausible dynamic evolution. In this work, we revisit over-smoothing from the perspective of latent dynamical mode compression: under partial observation and single-realization supervision, multiple plausible future modes can be weakened, merged, or averaged during forecasting. Based on this view, we propose Dirichlet-Guided Group Forecasting (DGF), a mode-preserving forecasting framework that explicitly models multiple mode-conditioned predictive distributions and uncertainty over their selection probabilities. DGF uses a Dirichlet-guided hierarchical sampling mechanism and reward-based optimization to encourage forecasts that are accurate, dynamically consistent, and mode-distinct. Extensive experiments on real-world forecasting benchmarks show that DGF reduces over-smoothing while improving forecasting accuracy, diversity, and dynamical consistency. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Zh-XY22/DGF

Current portfolio construction methods are either agnostic to the effects of idiosyncratic shocks (standard factor models) or to the latent data structure driving systematic returns (recent graph-based approaches). This presents an opportunity to combine the complementary market aspects captured by the factor and graph domains, allowing asset allocations to operate directly on the underlying market structure, rather than on its observed co-movement or its finite-sample artefacts. In this work, we introduce the Mutually-INformed Graph-Locality and Exposures framework (MINGLE), which mutually regularises the factor and graph domains by redefining graph locality through systematic factor exposure profiles, rather than via observed co-movements. This is formalised through a unified Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) framework that jointly learns a latent factor representation and its induced graph topology directly from market returns. The resulting exposure-similarity graph aligns more closely with established economic sectors than conventional correlation-based graphs. Portfolios constructed from this representation are shown to consistently outperform their correlation-based counterparts across a range of volatility regimes and transaction cost levels. For rigour, paired statistical testing confirms that these gains stem from the reconciliation of the graph and factor domains.

♻ ☆ ReCALM: A Residual-enhanced Crowdsourced Analytic Learning Mechanism for Distributed Continual Service Construction
Kejia Fan, Yajiang Huang, Jianheng Tang, Jinfeng Xu, Huiping Zhuang, Anfeng Liu, Houbing Herbert Song, Yunhuai Liu
Crowdsourcing has emerged as a promising paradigm for constructing AI services by harnessing the collective capabilities of distributed workers. As consumers' demands continually evolve, service models must acquire new knowledge while retaining previously learned information. However, due to the inherited reliance on gradients for backpropagation, existing approaches typically suffer from catastrophic forgetting during continual model updates on heterogeneous data. Recent studies have introduced analytic learning, a gradient-free paradigm that achieves invariance through recursive closed-form solutions. Nevertheless, existing analytic methods are typically constrained by single-layer linear networks, which tend to suffer from underfitting due to their inability to perform deep representation learning. To address this issue, we propose ReCALM, a Residual-enhanced Crowdsourced Analytic Learning Mechanism that achieves deep nonlinear invariance for distributed continual service construction. Inspired by the success of ResNet, we develop gradient-free residual blocks for ReCALM with closed-form solutions. To implement distributed continual training for ReCALM, we further devise a cross-recursive strategy via least squares. Both theoretical and experimental analyses verify ReCALM's dual superiority in heterogeneity invariance and deep representation. With 20 residual layers, ReCALM improves accuracy by 8.85%-9.83% over the single-layer analytic baseline, while reducing computational costs by over 94% compared with gradient-based baselines.
♻ ☆ HYPER: Hypothesis-Guided Planning for Evidence-Seeking Retrieval EACL 2027
Hangeol Chang, Changsun Lee, Seungjoon Rho, Junho Yeo, Jong Chul Ye
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) improves Large Language Models (LLMs) by grounding generation in external, non-parametric knowledge. However, when a task requires choosing among competing possibilities, such as a diagnosis among plausible alternatives, topically relevant context is often insufficient to drive the final decision. To address this issue, we propose HYPER: Hypothesis-Guided Planning for Evidence-Seeking Retrieval, a training-free pre-retrieval planning framework that reorients RAG from topic-oriented retrieval to evidence-oriented retrieval. HYPER uses a provisional answer hypothesis as a planning anchor. It then decomposes retrieval into three evidence roles. Support seeks evidence for the provisional answer. Distinction retrieves criteria that separate competing alternatives. Feature grounds salient question features needed for the decision. This planning step steers retrieval toward evidence near the decision boundary, enabling the generator to answer from context that is more directly aligned with the required choice. On MedQA and MMLU-Med, where single-query retrieval falls below no-retrieval chain-of-thought prompting, HYPER achieves the best average accuracy among ten baselines, improving over Simple RAG by 5.9 and 3.6 points, respectively. Its gains transfer to the 14 subjects of MMLU-Pro, at the cost of two additional LLM calls per question. Code is available at https://github.com/hangeol/HypothesisRAG.

♻ ☆ MUSE: Multi-Tenant Model Serving With Seamless Model Updates AAAI 2027
Cláudio Correia, Alberto E. A. Ferreira, Lucas Martins, Miguel P. Bento, Sofia Guerreiro, Ricardo Ribeiro Pereira, Ana Sofia Gomes, Jacopo Bono, Hugo Ferreira, Pedro Bizarro
In binary classification systems, decision thresholds translate model scores into actions. Choosing suitable thresholds relies on the specific distribution of the underlying model scores but also on the specific business decisions of each client using that model. However, retraining models inevitably shifts score distributions, invalidating existing thresholds. In multi-tenant Score-as-a-Service environments, where decision boundaries reside in client-managed infrastructure, this creates a severe bottleneck: recalibration requires coordinating threshold updates across hundreds of clients, consuming excessive human hours and leading to model stagnation. We introduce MUSE, a model serving framework that enables seamless model updates by decoupling model scores from client decision boundaries. Designed for multi-tenancy, MUSE optimizes infrastructure re-use by sharing models via dynamic intent-based routing, combined with a two-level score transformation that maps model outputs to a stable, reference distribution. Deployed at scale by Feedzai, MUSE processes over 4 thousand events per second, and over 55 billion events in the last 12 months, across several dozens of tenants, while maintaining high-availability and low-latency guarantees. By reducing model lead time from weeks to minutes, MUSE promotes model resilience against shifting attacks, saving millions of dollars in fraud losses and operational costs.

♻ ☆ Explanations that Transfer: Interpreting Medical Retrieval with Sparse AutoEncoders ML4H 2026
Diane Bouchacourt, Gaëtan Brison
Medical AI systems that answer users' queries rely on retrieving medical knowledge from large document collections. In this context, finetuning general models on medical datasets can improve retrieval relevance. Yet the dense embeddings underlying modern retrieval systems remain largely opaque, making it difficult to understand the mechanics behind their results. Moreover, adapting to a specific medical dataset risks losing transferability to new clinical corpora. In this work, we tackle these issues by applying Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to medical information retrieval, transforming dense text embeddings into semantically interpretable representations. To do so, our model combines a reconstruction objective with an InfoNCE contrastive loss that directly preserves query-document relevance. We evaluate three embedding models across six medical retrieval datasets, both in-domain and out-of-domain. Trained on a medical corpus, our sparse codes improve in-domain retrieval over the original embeddings, and lose less out-of-domain performance than their dense counterparts, especially when the target corpus is distant from the training one. Importantly, our experiments show that the method yields interpretable features whose semantic content can be inferred from the queries and documents that activate them most strongly. The interpretation of these features sheds light on why a particular document was retrieved, and transfers beyond the training distribution.

♻ ☆ Training-Free Dynamic Upcycling of Expert Language Models NeurIPS 2026
Eros Fanì, Oğuzhan Ersoy
Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable performance on a wide range of specialized tasks, exhibiting strong problem-solving capabilities. However, training these models is prohibitively expensive, and they often lack domain-specific expertise because they rely on general knowledge datasets. Expertise finetuning can address this issue; however, it often leads to overspecialization, and developing a single multi-domain expert remains difficult due to diverging objectives. Furthermore, multitask training is challenging due to interference and catastrophic forgetting. Existing work proposes combining the expertise of dense models within a Mixture of Experts (MoE) architecture, although this approach still requires multitask finetuning. To address these issues, we introduce Dynamic Upcycling MoE (DUME), a novel approach that reuses dense experts trained on different domains to construct a unified MoE model. Our method builds a single multitask model that preserves the capabilities of the original dense experts without requiring additional training. DUME is both cost-efficient and scalable: by leveraging the closed-form solution of ridge regression, it eliminates the need for further optimization and enables experts to be added or removed dynamically. Our extensive experiments on different tasks (in causal language modeling and reasoning settings) with several model sizes (between 115M and 9B parameters) and architectures demonstrate that DUME consistently outperforms baseline approaches. In particular, in a reasoning setting, DUME can also surpass the dense expert model's performance in its domain, achieving 104% of the dense expert's performance on average. Finally, we also show that the DUME model can be fine-tuned to further improve performance in complex reasoning scenarios. Our code is available at: github.com/gensyn-ai/dume.

♻ ☆ Probabilistic State Space Enumeration in Neural Network Computation
Victor O. K. Li, Yang Han, Jacqueline C. K. Lam
Many methods for pruning neural networks rank weights or groups of weights by importance and retain a single subset. We study how channel groups contribute jointly to the output of multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) in Transformer language models. Inspired by network reliability analysis, probabilistic state space enumeration (PSSE) represents the dense MLP output as the expected importance-corrected masked output over $2^G$ joint states of $G$ channel groups. Summing the most probable states' probability-weighted outputs gives an approximation whose absolute error is bounded by the omitted probability mass times the maximum masked-output norm. NORDER-II adapts ORDER-II to enumerate states in decreasing probability without sorting the full space. Its first $B$ states maximize the probability mass captured at that budget. A weight-entropy scorer fixes each layer's ordering from pretrained weights. We evaluate all 168 MLP layers across six models from the Llama, Gemma, and Qwen families on two datasets with 8, 16, and 32 channel groups. In all 1,008 comparisons, the 95%-mass prefix yields lower mean relative error than uniform sampling at the same state count, with or without bias correction. At all three group counts, it also yields lower median and 99th-percentile relative error than a single top-$k$ mask. For downstream inference, we use the number of distinct channels in each prefix to set pruned MLP widths. With one validation-selected group count per model, PSSE achieves lower perplexity than both top-$k$ pruning baselines in all 36 matched-FLOP settings. Our pruned decoder MLPs achieve mean speedups of $1.11\times$, $1.23\times$, and $1.36\times$ over dense MLPs at 10%, 20%, and 30% target MLP projection FLOP savings, respectively. PSSE offers a principled path toward both probability-mass-controlled approximation and more efficient inference in pretrained language models.
♻ ☆ Reinforcement Learning with Reference-Based Rewards for Language Model Reasoning and Alignment
Shuai Zhao, Yunqiu Xu, Linchao Zhu, Ling Chen, Yi Yang
Reinforcement learning (RL) powers two major lines of large language model (LLM) post-training: reasoning, which elicits deliberate, verifiable problem solving, and alignment, which steers models toward helpful, harmless, and honest behavior. Both hinge on reward design. Reasoning relies on rule-based verification of final answers, whose binary feedback is blind to intermediate derivations, whereas process reward models (PRMs) require step-level annotations too costly to scale. Alignment depends on reward models (RMs) trained on binary preference pairs, making both data collection and model training resource-intensive. We propose RL2R, reinforcement learning with reference-based rewards, as a unified and inexpensive alternative. Using pre-existing or distilled references, RL2R measures semantic similarity with lightweight metrics such as BERTScore between a sampled generation and a reference answer or solution. Similarity preserves ordinal quality signals that binary feedback discards: responses closer to the reference earn higher rewards, and sound derivations receive credit even when the final conclusion is wrong. For mathematical reasoning, augmenting rule-based verification with answer- and step-level similarity provides low-cost process supervision and outperforms answer-only verification. For alignment, a critic-free REINFORCE-style instantiation covers general preference, safety, and confidence tasks on par with RM-based methods. Reference-based rewards thus offer a cost-effective, versatile reward source spanning reasoning and alignment.
comment: The code is at https://github.com/mzhaoshuai/RL2R. This version adds a reasoning part with reference-based rewards compared to the previous version
♻ ☆ When Is Accuracy Evidence? A Unified Theory of Generalisation, Validation, and Information Fusion
JM Gorriz
K-fold cross-validation (CV) is widely used as evidence of out-of-sample performance, although folds are neither independent experiments nor equally informative under heterogeneous data. Cross Upper-Bound Validation (CUBV) replaces point-wise CV accuracy by conservative upper bounds on true risk. Here we generalise CUBV through a single exponential framework in which the moment-generating function of the generalisation gap is controlled by a cumulant envelope gamma(lambda). This yields a family of risk bounds covering Hoeffding-, Bernstein-, dependency-aware, PAC-Bayesian, and heterogeneous source-fusion settings. For K-fold CV, dependence between fold-wise gaps is modelled through a joint sub-Gaussian proxy matrix. Under equicorrelation, this gives an effective number of folds, Keff = K/[1+(K-1)rho], showing that increasing K does not necessarily increase statistical evidence when folds are strongly dependent. The framework is also extended to posterior distributions over predictors and weighted multi-source fusion, where weights are selected by minimising an upper bound on future risk rather than empirical error alone. Experiments with trained linear classifiers on heterogeneous multimodal Gaussian mixtures compare K-fold CV with full-sample resubstitution plus risk correction. Bounds are evaluated by coverage and tightness. In low-dimensional small-sample settings, K-fold partitioning can increase uncertainty because individual folds under-represent minority modes, while corrected resubstitution can remain valid and tighter; this effect disappears as sample size increases. Overall, gamma-CUBV separates observed performance, uncertainty, dependence, model complexity, and confidence into explicit terms, providing a unified route from CV scores to risk statements and a principled validation criterion for heterogeneous small-sample applications such as neuroimaging.

♻ ☆ Optimistic Actor-Critic with Parametric Policies for Linear Markov Decision Processes AISTATS 2026
Max Qiushi Lin, Reza Asad, Kevin Tan, Haque Ishfaq, Csaba Szepesvari, Sharan Vaswani
Although actor-critic methods have been successful in practice, their theoretical analyses have several limitations. Specifically, existing theoretical work either sidesteps the exploration problem by making strong assumptions or analyzes impractical methods with complicated algorithmic modifications. Moreover, the actor-critic methods analyzed for linear MDPs often employ natural policy gradient and define "implicit" policies through the accumulated critic estimates, rather than learning an explicitly parameterized actor. Such policies can be computationally expensive to sample from, making the environment interactions inefficient. To that end, we focus on the finite-horizon linear MDPs and propose an optimistic actor-critic framework that uses parametric log-linear policies. In particular, we introduce a tractable logit-matching regression objective for the actor. For the critic, we use approximate Thompson sampling via Langevin Monte Carlo to obtain optimistic value estimates. We prove that, when the policy features are sufficiently expressive, the resulting algorithm achieves $\widetilde{O}(ε^{-4})$ and $\widetilde{O}(ε^{-2})$ sample complexity in the on-policy and off-policy settings, respectively. Our results match the state-of-the-art dependence on $ε$ in prior theoretical work, while our algorithm is more aligned with practice.

♻ ☆ RiskWorld: Risk-Aware World Modeling with Flow-Guided Occupancy Evolution for Selective Trajectory Planning in Automated Driving
Rongxiang Zeng, Linsen Cai, Jiafu Zhang, Yijie Zhong, Yide Tao, Shuai Wang, Nan Zheng, Hai L. Vu, Alvaro Garcia Hernandez, Yongqi Dong
Safe motion planning in automated driving requires anticipating evolving traffic risks and deciding when to revise the current planned trajectory. We introduce RiskWorld, a risk-aware world modeling framework for shared occupancy forecasting and selective trajectory replacement. Spatial risk fields and temporal actor context are fused with visual bird's-eye-view features. Flow-guided evolution transports occupancy and scene features, while signed residuals correct occupancy after transport. One forecast is generated per planning step and reused across candidates. Each candidate is compared with a current-state persistence reference, yielding a nonnegative collision-score correction. The trajectory selected by current-world evaluation serves as the planning anchor and is replaced only when additional predicted risk triggers intervention and an alternative satisfies component-wise constraints on predicted risk and trajectory error. Candidate geometries remain unchanged. We evaluate RiskWorld for open-loop planning on nuScenes using camera features, annotation-derived current and historical actor states, and dataset-provided map context. RiskWorld achieves the lowest collision rate at a long evaluation horizon of 3 s, and the second-best average L2 error among various state-of-the-art baselines, while running at 11.5 FPS on a single NVIDIA RTX 4090 with 90.81 M parameters. Within-setting ablations show that RiskWorld achieves lower collision rates than the current-state rescoring baseline, while forecast reuse enables additional candidates to be evaluated at low marginal computational cost.

☆ Movie2Game-Bench: Holistic Evaluation of Film-to-Game Adaptation Beyond Playability
Jialing Xie, Yifan Zhou, Yiwen Zhang, Junjun He
Adapting a film into a game requires selecting source elements and translating them into player actions, rules, and feedback. We introduce Movie2Game-Bench (M2G-bench), a benchmark for evaluating film-to-game adaptation beyond playability. M2G-bench combines general evaluation, movie-specific evaluation, and playtesting by three GUI model players. The protocol connects source content to gameplay steps and implementation evidence, capturing both content preservation and interactive realization. The benchmark comprises 22 films and 658 source-specific reference items. Evaluating 14 models on the same films with their selected primary harnesses reveals complementary strengths in game quality, adaptation, and player experience. A shared weakness concerns playable sequences: this category has the lowest content-presence mean in all 14 models, averaging 37.9 out of 100 compared with 54.8 for iconic elements. Among judgments of retained emotionaldevelopment content, narrative choices account for 60.0% and scenario operation for 7.2%. These findings identify two linked priorities for film-to-game adaptation: preserving source situations that can support gameplay and connecting retained content to player actions and consequences.

Daiqing Wu, Junqiao Wang, Chengyang Fang, Runhao Zeng, Fei Ma, Sicheng Zhao

☆ Worth Another Look:Constrained World-Model Planning for Visual Inspection

Ultimately, pairing lightweight learned dynamics with exact symbolic constraints turns frozen detectors into adaptive, budget-aware inspection agents without retraining.

Evaluating this capability therefore requires assessing whether models can translate opportunities for interaction into better understanding. We focus on high-frame-rate action videos, where rapid, subtle changes make targeted observation especially valuable. The benchmark comprises 1,000 multiple-choice questions spanning six categories of fine-grained action understanding, accompanied by temporal evidence annotations and user hints screened for answer leakage. We evaluate single-pass observation, autonomous tool use, and tool use combined with user feedback to examine how effectively models exploit these opportunities. Evaluation of five models reveals distinct patterns in how they acquire evidence and respond to opportunities for further interaction. These findings establish VideoACE as a testbed for examining agentic video understanding beyond performance under a fixed observation setting.

Animating virtual opponents is an important yet challenging task in game development. In martial arts games, opponent motions must not only be physically plausible but also exhibit appropriate technique, timing, transitions, and target-directed intent. Traditional game animations often rely on handcrafted clips, state machine transitions, and procedural adjustments, which can be labor-intensive and may limit the behavioral diversity of non-player characters. To demonstrate their applicability to interactive gameplay, we developed a VR sparring prototype for Meta Quest headsets. The prototype combines policy-generated motion clips with lightweight state-based control to support interactive opponent behavior. Together, these findings support the feasibility of using a learned martial arts skill repertoire as a motion foundation for animating opponents in VR sparring games.
♻ ☆ Learning Binary Codes with Spiking Neural Networks for Cross-Modal Hashing Retrieval
Yukuan Zhang, Jiarui Zhao, Shangqing Nie, Jin Kuang, Dong Liu, Shengsheng Wang
Cross-modal hashing (CMH) uses compact binary codes for efficient image-text retrieval. Most methods learn image-text relationships in a continuous space and binarize the representation only at the end. Semantic learning and bit decisions thus remain largely separate. This work addresses two key questions concerning hash-bit generation: \textbf{(1) How to determine hash bits?} We leverage the discrete nature of spiking activity and determine each bit through competition between positive and negative spikes accumulated over time, rather than through a single firing event or subsequent thresholding of continuous representations. \textbf{(2) How to generate such hash bits?} We propose an unsupervised spiking framework for cross-modal hashing, in which image and text jointly contribute to hash-bit generation through temporal interaction. Extensive experiments on three benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach and support temporal spike competition as a design principle for hash-code generation.

Our introduced dual domains facial landmark detection framework can solve the lack of accurate facial landmark coordinates during the AU domain separation and reconstruction training process, while the parameters of homostructural facial extraction modules from these two similar facial tasks are shared. Moreover, we propose a pixel-level feature alignment scheme to maintain the consistency of features obtained from two separation and reconstruction processes. Furthermore, a weighted asymmetric loss is proposed to change the contribution of positive and negative samples of each type of AUs to model parameters updating. Experimental results on three widely used benchmarks demonstrate our superiority to most state-of-the-art methods for AU detection.
♻ ☆ Auditing Hyperstimulation at Scale in Child-Facing YouTube Videos
Shao-Yu Chu, Qiyu Li, Xuan Liu, Shuang Hao, Haojian Jin
Parents, pediatricians, and journalists have raised concern that child-facing videos are becoming increasingly stimulating (faster-paced, louder, and more visually dense), but this concern rests mostly on ad hoc observation rather than systematic measurement. We present a large-scale audit of hyperstimulation patterns, which we refer to as content-independent production choices, such as rapid cutting, that may place demands on children's developing cognitive and sensory processing capacities. Drawing on parents' Reddit discussions and developmental psychology, we develop computational metrics for 12 hyperstimulation patterns. We apply these metrics to 16,375 videos from 542 child-facing YouTube channels spanning 2015-2026. We found broad increases in stimulation over time, with cut rates rising across all five content categories. Nearly a quarter of the channels increased in at least one stimulation pattern over time. More stimulating videos also tended to receive more views, but the relevant stimulation patterns differed across content types.
♻ ☆ FLARE: Full-Modality Long-Video Audiovisual Retrieval Benchmark with User-Simulated Queries NeurIPS 2026
Qijie You, Hao Liang, Mingrui Chen, Bohan Zeng, Meiyi Qiang, Zhenhao Wong, Wentao Zhang
As video becomes increasingly central to information dissemination and multimodal large language models (MLLMs) continue to advance, evaluating video retrieval has become increasingly important. In realistic search scenarios, this requires matching short user queries to long-form content using both visual and auditory evidence. Yet existing retrieval benchmarks are still dominated by short clips, single modalities, and caption-based evaluation. We introduce FLARE, a full-modality long-video audiovisual retrieval benchmark with user-simulated queries. Built from 399 carefully screened Video-MME videos (10--60 min, 225.4 h) to ensure source quality and diversity, FLARE contains 87,697 clips annotated with vision, audio, and unified audiovisual captions, together with 274,933 user-style queries. Cross-modal queries are further filtered by a hard bimodal constraint, requiring retrieval to fail under either modality alone but succeed when both are combined. FLARE evaluates models under two regimes, caption-based and query-based retrieval, across vision, audio, and unified audiovisual settings. Experiments with 15 representative retrievers show that user-style queries substantially change model behavior, strong caption-based performance does not always transfer to query-based retrieval, and audio--language alignment remains a key bottleneck for unified audiovisual retrieval. Our code and data are released at https://flarebench.github.io/

♻ ☆ Lifting 3D Gaussians: A Wavelet Multiresolution Representation for Scalable Gaussian Splatting Streaming
Yuang Shi, Géraldine Morin, Simone Gasparini, Wei Tsang Ooi
3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) represents a scene as an unstructured set of primitives optimized at a single scale, offering no native support for progressive delivery to heterogeneous devices. Existing scalable approaches organize these primitives into independent quality layers or spatial hierarchies. However, maintaining separate splat representations across scales introduces redundancy, while independent layers have limited ability to correct coarse geometry as finer detail arrives. We present LiftGS, a multiresolution representation that organizes a scene into a coarse Gaussian set and a tree of refinements. Each refinement replaces one coarse Gaussian with two finer children whose attributes are learned relative to their parent. Inspired by wavelet lifting, we encode these changes using a shared detail vector and per-attribute factors that allow the two children to differ asymmetrically from the parent. A client first receives the coarse set, then reconstructs and substitutes children as refinement data arrives. This construction reuses previously transmitted attributes to encode finer detail and removes replaced parents from the active rendering set, reducing both refinement payload and rendering memory. Extensive experiments on four benchmark datasets show LiftGS cuts splat redundancy from over 65% to under 25%, reduces transmission payload and GPU memory by up to 2.4x and 5.5x over state-of-the-art scalable-3DGS baselines, achieves smooth quality transitions in simulated progressive delivery, and compresses a further 8.7x with standard coding at negligible quality loss. Project website: https://yuang-ian.github.io/liftgs/

In side-by-side human evaluation, Kandinsky 6.0 Video Pro clearly outperforms its predecessor, Kandinsky 5.0 Video Pro, and remains competitive with leading audio-video generation models, outperforming LTX 2.5 and Seedance 2.0 in speech quality. ☆ Ambient LLMs: Data-Efficient Supervised Fine-tuning via Temperature Matching
Giannis Daras, Marios Papachristou, Adam Klivans, Antonio Torralba, Constantinos Daskalakis
Collecting large-scale, diverse, and high-quality post-training datasets for autoregressive language models is challenging. Consequently, Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) is typically applied to datasets significantly smaller than those used for pre-training, which leads to overfitting and the catastrophic forgetting of the tails of the data distribution. To prevent this collapse, we introduce Ambient SFT, a principled framework for leveraging imperfect predictions to augment the fine-tuning set. In our method, a "frozen" version of the pre-trained model serves as a noisy teacher that the fine-tuned model must match at a coarse level. In particular, we require that the high-temperature versions of the conditional distributions produced by the post-training model should match the high-temperature versions of the pre-training ones. The temperature hyperparameter controls the level of trust in the pre-trained model, with the limit $T\to \infty$ reverting back to regular SFT and $T=1$ to knowledge distillation. We demonstrate that our approach outperforms standard SFT across domain adaptation, instruction-tuning, and reasoning, leading for up to $21\%$ average relative improvement to standard SFT.

☆ What Does a Bias Head Measure? Non-Identifiability in Head-Level Bias Attribution ACL
S. M Seefat Alam
Methods that localise social bias in large language models to individual attention heads and remove it by ablation are validated by their effect on a fairness metric, never by evidence that the statistic selecting the heads measures bias. We audit this on Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. The head map correlates at $ρ= -0.950$ and $-0.768$ with a label-blind response-length map, apparently identifying a surface confound. An intervention that breaks the length-label coupling rejects this reading: with the prompt held fixed, response length explains 1% of the statistic's variance. What does explain it is prompt identity, at 64% of variance, in an ordering that is not monotonic in length. Within any fixed prompt the fairness label, response length and the presence of a protected-group token are collinear at $φ= 0.95$, partly by definition of the labelling rule, so no observational analysis can attribute the map to any of them, and no method in this family performs an experiment that could. The substantive claims fail independently: bias selectivity is not late-layer-concentrated on either model under either reference reading, and no head set we tested reduces the unfairness rate when ablated. Its complement, scored on the opposite label, reliably destroys refusal behaviour ($p = 2.7\times10^{-5}$), demonstrating that the pipeline detects effects at this scale.

☆ Structure--Residual Inductive Biases for Language Model Pretraining
Hai Huang, Bartosz Żuk, Rassul Magauin, Jiaxin Huang, Xue Liu
Next-token prediction is relied upon to learn both predictive behavior and internal representations. We ask whether representation structure itself should be an explicit inductive bias. Motivated by the two-part coding view of Kolmogorov complexity, we study a structure--residual principle in which a representation separates structure from realization detail. We instantiate this principle in two complementary ways. Boundary Bottleneck Concept (BBC) routes information from token segments through boundary carriers while preserving local autoregressive computation. Continuous Concept (CC) regularizes representation geometry and induces a spectral decomposition into low-frequency structure and high-frequency residual. We derive coding bounds for both views and show that multiplicity-corrected boundary attention becomes exact as the within-segment path energy vanishes. Empirically, BBC and CC exhibit strikingly different depth preferences: BBC works best in early layers, whereas CC is most effective in later layers. At 300M training tokens, combining BBC and CC improves NLL by 1.44\% on GPT-2 Medium. These gains persist with training runs up to 20B tokens. Representation diagnostics show that BBC increases the relative predictive importance of boundary states, while CC reduces spectral residual energy. Together, these results suggest that structure--residual biases can improve language-model pretraining beyond next-token prediction. Code: https://github.com/haihuang-ml/structure-residual
☆ Polarity Composition Hypothesis: Causal Evidence from Negation in NLI EACL 2027
Nhi Hoai Doan, Tatsuya Hiraoka, Munachiso Samuel Nwadike, Kentaro Inui
We investigate how language models process negation in natural language inference (NLI). We propose the \textit{Polarity Composition Hypothesis}, a high-level causal model of this computation. Behavioral evaluations show that language-model predictions largely conform to the proposed hypothesis. Using Distributed Alignment Search, we identify causally effective subspaces aligned with the variables in the polarity-composition hypothesis. These representations transfer across negation forms and partially to a subset of MNLI. We release the dataset and code.

☆ MoE--LoRA Methods for Multilingual Adaptation: A Systematic Empirical Study EACL 2027
Nikit Srivastava, Joel Dag, René Speck, Axel-Cyrille Ngonga Ngomo
Routed low-rank adapters offer a parameter-efficient means to improve the performance of large language models (LLMs) across tasks. Hence, it is assumed that they can also be used to improve the support of low-resource languages in LLMs, which currently serve English far better than the thousands of other languages spoken worldwide. However, this assumption has never been verified empirically under a shared multilingual evaluation protocol. We address exactly this gap by comparing eight low-rank adaptation (LoRA) methods on a frozen base model using 200 unique languages in more than 9{,}000 evaluation settings. Our results suggest that a reduced-scale search can identify viable configurations of LoRA methods but does not reliably predict their relative performance, as the top-ranking configuration is never best at scale. LoRA reliably improves language-model fit on translation data, consistently degrades reading comprehension, and benefits low-resource languages most. These findings suggest that LoRA methods should be regarded as targeted tools rather than general-purpose means for improving the multilingual capabilities of LLMs.

☆ TextSphere: Efficient Text-to-Image Generation via Shared Hyperspherical Alignment and Uniformity
Yixia Zhang, Girish A. Koushik, Xilu Wang, Wenwu Wang
Recent advances in text-to-image generation have substantially improved image quality, particularly through diffusion-based methods that require multiple inference steps. In contrast, Sphere Encoder offers an efficient generative framework capable of producing images with fewer forward steps. However, extending it to free-form text is nontrivial, because its class-conditioned design lacks cross-modal alignment. To address this challenge, we propose TextSphere, an efficient text-to-image generative framework that extends Sphere Encoder with language conditioning and cross-modal alignment. We incorporate pretrained CLIP text embeddings through adaptive layer normalization (AdaLN) to guide image generation while retaining the original spherical sampling mechanism. To bridge the cross-modal representation gap, we introduce a Spherical Semantic Alignment and Uniformity (SSAU) objective that jointly promotes semantic alignment and representation uniformity on the hypersphere. Experiments on CUB-200-2011, MS-COCO-2014, and Flickr30k demonstrate that TextSphere consistently reduces generation FID (gFID) over the text-conditioned baseline while achieving reconstruction FID (rFID) below 1.0. With only 4 and 6 sampling steps, TextSphere achieves lower gFID than the compared diffusion- and GAN-based models trained from scratch on CUB-200-2011 and MS-COCO-2014, respectively. We further observe that improved reconstruction fidelity does not necessarily yield better generation quality. In addition, we use Partial Least Squares Singular Value Decomposition (PLS-SVD) to analyze cross-modal alignment and modality gap, offering insight into the effectiveness of our approach.

☆ Mind the Gap: A Deployed Multi-Agent System for Documentation Maintenance AAAI 2027
Lorenzo Masoero
The "AI revolution" has enabled teams across the technology industry to deliver software features at unprecedented velocity. While code evolves faster than ever, customer-facing documentation often struggles to stay up to speed. As users increasingly rely on LLM-based agents that consume documentation as their primary interface, the impact of this documentation gap worsens: stale information propagates and is treated as authoritative. Signals for identifying where documentation has fallen behind already exist in abundance, both explicit (e.g., resolved support tickets revealing what documentation lacks) and implicit (e.g., code-documentation discrepancies detectable from automated loops). We deploy a multi-agent system, built around a triage agent we call "TriAgent," that continuously extracts these signals and repairs documentation drift. Over 43 days of shadow-mode operation, our system triaged 499 tickets and surfaced 92 gaps in the documentation. Using a panel of LLM judges from independent model families, 81.1% of TriAgent's verifiable assertions were correct (245 of the 302 assertions the human resolution addresses; majority of three judges); on length-comparable pairs the panel preferred TriAgent's response in 70.5% of pairs and the human engineer's in 23.2% (the rest had no judge majority). Importantly, agent- and human-sourced replies tended to be complementary, with the human often surfacing insights that were either buried within the existing documentation or missing from it entirely; our system turns each such insight into a documentation gap and, after human review, a fix. Repairing a gap measurably improved the agent's later answer: when the agent re-answered the same ticket after the repair, blinded judges preferred the post-repair answer over its own pre-repair answer 71.4% of the time (n=35). A blinded human audit confirms strong alignment on self-improvement.

☆ The Illusion of Grounding: Do Vision-Language Models Weigh Retrieved Text and Images Like an Ideal Observer?
Basavaraj R M, Harshal Chandel
Retrieval-augmented vision-language models (VLMs) answer from two sources of evidence that can each fail: the retrieved text can be wrong or noisy, and the image can be degraded or contradicted. We introduce GIB-200K, 200,000 image-question items built from COCO and Visual Genome, each expanded into controlled stress conditions: hard-negative retrieval noise (1-20 documents), visual ambiguity (Gaussian and motion blur, low-resource crops) and cross-modal conflict with counterfactual flip pairs. Instead of only measuring degradation, we ask how models combine the two modalities. From ideal Bayesian cue combination we derive a testable prediction that yields formal definitions of Knowledge Inertia (text over-weighted relative to the model's own image evidence) and Sensory Capture (the reverse), and we estimate the weights with a measurement-error-corrected regression whose recovery of known weights we verify. A counterfactual flip decomposition separates modality bias from concept priors, and a Grounding Illusion Score measures how much clean accuracy is not grounded in the image. We evaluate 4 open models on one frozen, seeded evaluation split of 2,000 GIB-200K items. All models are accurate on clean inputs (92.5%-94.2%) but adverse accuracy falls to 41.3%-59.9%. The two LLaVA models over-weight the text (Knowledge Inertia, w_T/w_I = 1.229 and 1.322), whereas InternVL3 favours the image (w_T/w_I = 0.680); between 34.8% and 71.4% of the clean answers that are correct are abandoned when the document lies. A training-free consistency check that compares the answer with and without retrieval trades coverage for accuracy under misleading documents, while falling back to the image fails when the image is heavily degraded. All per-instance outputs, code, and an audit that recomputes every reported open-model number are released.

☆ Dynamic Task Allocation with Dialogue IROS 2026
Matthew Groholski, Weiwei Gu, Nakul Gopalan
Effective multi-agent collaboration requires agents to adapt task allocation as goals and responsibilities evolve. Prior task-allocation frameworks often assume static goals, full observability, or rely on large language models (LLMs) without explicit, verifiable beliefs about task allocation or intent. These assumptions limit their applicability to real-world collaboration, where agents often lack full information about each other's actions, progress, or local environment. To support dynamic task allocation under partial observability, we introduce a communication-augmented Bayesian task-allocation framework. Our agent uses dialogue to reduce uncertainty about the environment and collaborators, while keeping decisions grounded in explicit probabilistic beliefs. We evaluate our framework in an Overcooked domain extended with dynamically arriving tasks under both full and partial object-space observability. Our communication agent consistently outperforms a vanilla LLM agent in both settings. Additionally, our framework performs comparably to a non-communicating task-allocation baseline under full observability, but substantially outperforms it under partial observability as task complexity increases by an average speed up of 0.585 and completes on average 18 timesteps faster. These results indicate that our agent is more efficient in dynamic task allocation than baselines in partially observable environments, and that communication is important as available information decreases.

☆ Nunchi: Ears Help Eyes in Multi-Party Conversations
JunYeong Park, Shijing Wang, Seonwook Park, Michael Stengel, Shalini De Mello, Sang-Il Choi, Hyung Jin Chang
Identifying whom a person looks at is central to understanding multi-party conversations, yet gaze geometry alone becomes ambiguous as more people appear. Conversations offer cues that geometry lacks, such as who is speaking and what is said, but no gaze dataset provides them for many multi-party scenes. We introduce SORBET, a benchmark of 3,340 samples from 1,578 clips with synchronized speech, transcripts, and attended person labels, covering more multi-party scenes than existing gaze datasets. Prior gaze models struggle to use these cues, which come in different forms, must be linked to the right person, and can conflict with gaze geometry. We propose Nunchi, a framework that constructs a text prompt from the transcript and the outputs of gaze and speaker models, links every cue to the candidates with shared labels, and lets a vision-language model (VLM) weigh gaze geometry against conversational cues to identify the attended person. Nunchi outperforms the strongest existing method by 4.8 percentage points. On SORBET, conversational cues help whereas additional visual cues do not, and the gains hold across three VLMs, with automatic transcripts, and on two existing datasets.

☆ Large-scale Neuron Community Discovery Reveals Neuron-Sparse Behaviors in Language Models
Igor Shilov, Thomas Fel, Tal Haklay, Lucius Bushnaq, Owen Lewis
What reusable units of computation can we discover within a language model's neurons? Prior work has shown that individual forward passes can often be sparsified post-hoc to small groups of neurons, but it has been unclear whether these groups form coherent computational entities reused across inputs. We introduce neuron community discovery, an unsupervised method for finding neuron groups that recur across prompts and are causally necessary and sufficient, within the layers they span, for common computations. The method combines gradient-based attribution, a graph connecting neurons that are repeatedly attributed together, and community detection. Applied to Llama-3.1-8B using ten million prompts, it discovers thousands of candidate communities. We evaluate them on held-out prompts through three causal tests: community necessity, sufficiency within a layer subset, and layer necessity. These tests identify groups whose removal disrupts predictions and whose retention preserves predictions despite ablating the remaining MLP neurons in the tested layers. Discovered communities support functions like grammatical agreement, token-probability calibration, fixed phrases, in-context copying, addition, and multiplication. With communities capped at 128 neurons across all layers, 10.3% of held-out prompts have at least one layer's contribution explained on a neuron-sparse basis. Coverage remains 8.7% when requiring at least four layers and 3.3% when requiring at least twelve. These results show that small groups of existing neurons can provide reusable computational components across prompts, and that such groups can be discovered at scale.
☆ Natural Language Programming: Rethinking Language, Memory, and Cognition in the Era of Generative AI
Giovanni Adorni, Daniele Grosso
Generative Artificial Intelligence is transforming the role of natural language in computational systems. In classical Natural Language Processing (NLP), language was treated as an object of computation: something to analyse, classify, translate, or generate. Large Language Models (LLMs) challenge this perspective, enabling natural language to function increasingly as an executable cognitive medium through which humans structure reasoning, orchestrate problem solving, and regulate hybrid human/AI workflows. This paper introduces Natural Language Programming (NLPg) as a theoretical and epistemological extension of traditional NLP. Rather than focusing on language understanding alone, NLPg conceptualises prompts as dynamic cognitive artefacts that externalise goals, constraints, assumptions, validation criteria, and intermediate reasoning states. Prompting is thus not merely a technical interaction technique, but a form of dialogic cognitive programming operating within distributed human/AI memory architectures. Building on theories of distributed cognition, extended mind, metacognition, and dialogic learning, the paper proposes the notion of Dialogic Working Memory, describing how prompts and conversational states function as temporary external memory structures supporting reasoning continuity and reflective regulation. We further map existing memory architectures (BTMA, SKGE, RMR) onto this framework, illustrating how episodic, semantic, and metacognitive layers support long-horizon conversational coherence. Finally, implications for computational linguistics and AI/mediated knowledge systems are discussed, suggesting a post symbolic and post interface paradigm in which natural language operates simultaneously as communication medium, executable specification, cognitive scaffold, and distributed memory architecture.

♻ ☆ Localized LoRA-MoE: Mixture of Low-Rank Experts With Adaptive Routing
Babak Barazandeh, Subhabrata Majumdar, Vinay Prithyani, George Michailidis
Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods such as LoRA adapt large models through a single low-rank update. Such updates are susceptible to gradient interference: when a training stream interleaves multiple operational contexts, conflicting updates to shared adapter weights collapse the adapter into an unspecialized average. While recent methods introduce block-wise isolation to remedy this issue, their topologies are static and cannot adapt to context switching or localized sensor degradation. In this work, we introduce Localized LoRA-MoE, a framework that combines localized spatial blocking with context-conditioned expert routing. We propose and evaluate two architectural variants: Block-Wise LoRA-MoE (centralized routing), which modulates the entire structural grid through a single context-conditioned gate, and Cell-Wise LoRA-MoE (decentralized routing), which assigns an independent gate to every coordinate cell of the matrix grid. Across three structured transformation benchmarks--a high-dimensional SVD matrix simulation, context-switched transformations over real tabular data, and spatial reconstruction under simulated sensor occlusion--both variants outperform static baselines under comparable adapter budgets. Both variants perform similarly when context shifts the grid uniformly, while cell-wise routing is strictly better when contexts are spatially heterogeneous. When fine-tuning a language model on six interleaved GLUE tasks, task-conditioned routing at a fixed adapter budget outperforms LoRA and static localized adapters, matching per-task adapters with 6x budgets. At decoder scale on Qwen2.5-1.5B, both routed variants outperform static baselines across eight commonsense benchmarks, with cell-wise routing achieving +3.9 points over LoRA at matched active capacity.

Small open-weight language models now run on a laptop, but they fail at multi-step work in ways a large model does not: they stop with the files missing, repeat one action until the budget ends, and report success without checking. At the one-to-nine-billion-parameter tier the harness supplies almost all of the procedural control that a large model supplies for itself.We present Mingbird, an open-source harness for that tier on a consumer graphics card: 12k lines of Python, a 628-test suite, and eighteen mechanisms for context economy, completion, time budget and the host boundary, plus a crawl guard outside those four groups. Its design point is completion control: the harness runs executable checks on the working directory and refuses a claim of completion when they fail.Five evaluations accompany it. A configuration-surface audit finds four defects that the 625-test suite of v3.1.1 missed, each because a test checked a property adjacent to the one that broke. A ten-task probe suite gives each mechanism a reason to fire and reports where the change reaches the artifact, including one mechanism that cuts the signal it protects. Disabling five of six completion-time checks costs 0.152 of the artifact score on eighteen held-out tasks, three replications per cell (95% CI [+0.064, +0.246], Holm p = 0.014). On a 288-cell matrix the harness reaches 0.886 against 0.631, 0.479 and 0.405 for three open scaffolds, and on τ 2 -bench it ranks first or tied first in all three domains against the arms evaluated.Tasks, scorer, source and every per-cell result are public.

♻ ☆ In-Context Optimization for Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Gradient-Descent Perspective NIPS 2026
Mingchen Li, Jiatan Huang, Chuxu Zhang, Liang Zhao, Hong Yu
In-context learning has recently been linked to implicit gradient descent in linear self-attention models, suggesting that context can induce a forward-pass update. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) also relies on context, but retrieved documents are usually treated as static evidence rather than signals for adaptation. We study RAG as an in-context optimization process. First, we show that one linear self-attention layer can implement one gradient-descent step on a unified linearized RAG objective covering both projection-based and dot-product retrieval interfaces. This gives an exact regime where retrieval-augmented prediction and in-context optimization coincide. We use this result not as a literal model of LLM computation, but as a guide for adapting the interaction between queries and retrieved evidence. We then test the boundary of this correspondence: it remains stable under controlled linear extensions, but becomes feature-distribution dependent under nonlinear architectures. Finally, we turn this view into a lightweight method for frozen RAG LLMs. The method keeps the retriever and backbone fixed, and predicts a context-conditioned update to a generator-side evidence-use interface. Across seven QA benchmarks, two retrievers, and two frozen LLM backbones, this forward-only update improves a shared-interface baseline, transfers to held-out tasks, and approaches test-time gradient adaptation at much lower per-query cost.
comment: NIPS 2026
♻ ☆ RICE-PO: Turning Retrieval Interactions into Credit Signals for Reasoning Agents NIPS 2026
Mingchen Li, Hansi Zeng, Zhuo Qian, Jiatan Huang, Sunjae Kwon, Hamed Zamani, Hong Yu
Retrieval is increasingly moving from one-shot matching toward interactive reasoning, where language agents iteratively inspect evidence, reformulate queries, and search again. Training such agents raises a credit-assignment challenge: executable actions such as queries or summaries can be directly evaluated by the retriever, while latent reasoning steps are not directly observable and only affect future executable actions. This asymmetry makes outcome-level reward assignment unreliable, as the same final reward may credit reasoning steps that did not actually shape retrieval success. We propose RICE-PO, a critic-free policy optimization framework that converts retrieval interactions into localized learning signals. RICE-PO selects high-uncertainty executable actions as anchors, evaluates local counterfactual branches using retrieval metrics, and propagates credit to latent reasoning steps only when reasoning-to-action influence is strong and future residual effects are stable. On BRIGHT and BEIR, RICE-PO consistently outperforms prompt-based agents and group-based RL baselines under the same retriever setting. These results show that the structure of agent-environment interaction itself can provide useful supervision for training reasoning-based retrieval agents.

♻ ☆ MamaReason: Unfinished Reasoning and Answer Recovery in Clinical Language Models
Thanni Adewuyi, Adepoju Jeremiah Moyondafoluwa, Dorcas Amapu, Dieko Whenu, Sylvia Essessien, Sandra Oko-Oba, Pelumi Onafadeji, Lily Aimas-Love, Samuel Omolaiye, AbdulQahhar Okenla, Abiodun Adereni
Answer continuation often returns a diagnosis already stated in unfinished clinical reasoning. We study this behavior in MamaReason, adapted from dense Gemma 4 31B, on MamaBench's 217 paired maternal and child-health presentations. An explicit-commitment extractor identifies a diagnosis in 75 of 94 failed RL first passes and 75 of 93 failed SFT first passes. The continuation matches that diagnosis in 67/75 RL cases and 58/75 SFT cases, using diagnosis strings alone. Reading these commitments without additional generation recovers 30 of the 40 RL pairs restored by continuation under the archived correctness labels. Recurrence controls distinguish routine mentions from repeated answer selection. An offline second-commitment trigger measures the tradeoff between earlier readout and paired accuracy. The resulting decomposition separates diagnostic content already present in a trace, completion of an accepted answer, and paired diagnostic correctness. For clinical language-model evaluation, these are distinct outcomes that become visible when the same reasoning trace is examined through multiple readouts.
♻ ☆ Asymmetric Discourse Homogenization on Reddit Was a Text-Length Artifact: A Reanalysis
Fengming Liu
In the first version of this paper I reported that conservative Reddit users began writing more alike after ChatGPT was released while progressive users did not. That result came from a similarity measure that rises and falls with comment length. I redo every analysis of the original paper on all 6,056,593 comments with a sentence encoder and a dispersion measure computed within length strata, and the conservative break goes away. The two camps show no reliable difference in how within-group similarity changed after late 2022, and the ChatGPT date behaves like any of the more than two thousand other cutoffs I test. The matched flair comparison, the cumulative AI index, the stayer panel and the entropy signature each lose their support once length is held fixed. The one change that survives is older. Left and right comments drew closer to each other between 2019 and 2022, and that convergence was complete before ChatGPT arrived. I end with what this implies for studies that measure homogenization with embeddings.
comment: 18 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables. This version replaces v1 entirely: the v1 headline finding (asymmetric conservative homogenization after ChatGPT) was an artifact of comment length in the similarity measure. The artifact is documented in general form in arXiv:2611.21519
♻ ☆ Continued Training of Continuous Language Flows with Token Identity Squared Supervision
Jiawei Jiang, Zhaoxiang Zang, Zhengtao Yu
Diffusion and flow models have recently been extended to language modeling, generating text through continuous denoising in token embedding spaces. Pretrained models provide token representations and contextual prediction capabilities, but improving generation with limited additional training requires an appropriate connection between supervision and continuous generation. When continuous predictions are formed by weighting token embeddings with predicted probabilities, different probability distributions can yield the same vector and are therefore indistinguishable under a continuous reconstruction objective based on mean squared error (MSE). We propose Token Identity Brier Flow (TIBF) to apply squared supervision directly to token identities. TIBF fixes token embeddings, combines network scores with token-matching scores under a Gaussian observation model, supervises token probabilities using the Brier loss, and uses probability-weighted embeddings for continuous generation. We show that, for fixed token embeddings, the squared error in token posterior prediction controls the squared errors of the continuous denoising prediction and the flow velocity. A risk decomposition separates uncertainty inherent in the observation from posterior fitting error, motivating continued training that preserves pretrained embeddings and focuses on probability prediction. From common pretrained initializations and under matched continuation budgets, TIBF achieves mean Gen.PPL values of 34.87 on OWT and 80.08 on LM1B, outperforming continuous-MSE and CE controls. Further evaluations show improvements across multiple sampling budgets. Code is available at https://github.com/Jiangjiawei-kust/TIBF.
comment: 49 pages, including appendices; 7 figures. Code: https://github.com/Jiangjiawei-kust/TIBF
♻ ☆ RL Post-Training Builds Compositional Reasoning Strategies NeurIPS 2026
Azwar Abdulsalam, Nishil Patel, Andrew Saxe
Does RL post-training merely amplify primitive skills already latent in a base model, or can it compose primitive skills into new higher-level strategies? We study this question in a fully observable rewrite-grammar environment where the pretraining distribution is known and every generated rewrite can be audited. A Transformer is pretrained on primitive symbol-rewrite chains and post-trained on a Trace-based reasoning task with only a binary final-answer reward. RL solves held-out problems that remain rarely solved by the pretrained model even under much larger sampling budgets, while rejection fine-tuning improves early but plateaus. Trace analysis shows that RL reorganizes primitive competence through a phased compositional mechanism: it first strengthens primitive reductions, then discovers valid composed procedures. These include sequential compositions, which collapse ordered chains of primitive contractions, and parallel compositions, which combine independent primitive contractions in a single step. The composed procedures are not isolated samples; they are reused and consolidated into a stable repertoire. Comparing RL with rejection fine-tuning shows that the key difference is not exploration volume but selectivity: RFT produces many shortcut-like rewrites, much of them invalid, whereas RL concentrates exploration into valid reusable structure. Pretraining ablations show that the emergence of compositional strategies is gated not by primitive exposure alone, but by whether pretraining organizes primitive competence into reduction procedures that RL can later compress. The base model provides weak procedural ingredients; RL builds them into reliable higher-level strategies.
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (poster)
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition
☆ Spool: Low-Latency Streaming Inference for Hybrid Vision-Language Models
Rui Ning, Om Chabra, Hari Balakrishnan
Applications such as visual accessibility agents and robotics require answering questions about recent video content promptly, over a bounded window of past frames (e.g., the last two minutes). Hybrid vision-language models (VLMs), which interleave attention with linear recurrent layers such as Gated DeltaNet (GDN), are attractive for this setting, but maintaining a sliding window is expensive. The reason is that recurrent layers combine all past frames into a shared state, so expiring old frames normally requires re-running the entire window through the model. We observe that the recurrent update is affine in the state with input-dependent coefficients, so the effect of each frame can be captured as a transformation that composes associatively. We present Spool, a training-free framework that caches per-frame state transformations and composes them efficiently as the window advances, removing expired frames from each recurrent layer's state without replaying frames through the backbone. Removal is exact within each layer; as with key-value eviction in attention, expired frames can retain residual influence through the cached inputs computed by earlier layers. We design a dedicated data structure and GPU kernels to achieve low caching and composition overhead. Across five open-source hybrid VLMs and four video reasoning benchmarks, Spool achieves the lowest p95 time-to-first-token in all 20 model-benchmark tests, reducing it by a geometric mean of $6.6\times$ over the faster of two recent vLLM baselines, while improving accuracy by 2.3 percentage points on average.
☆ FastFrames: Video Generation at Interactive Latency
Gene Chou, Guandao Yang, Fujun Luan, Lars Mescheder, Wei Dong, Stephan Richter, Vladlen Koltun
Autoregressive video diffusion models generate frames based on new observations and inputs, making them a promising medium for interactive visual experiences. However, existing models are orders of magnitude too slow for fluid interaction. This paper introduces FastFrames, a family of fast autoregressive video diffusion models that achieves interactive latency without compromising quality. We profile the inference pipeline of state-of-the-art models and find that operations often treated as fixed implementation details, such as VAE decoding and KV cache updates, in fact account for over half of end-to-end inference latency. We challenge the assumption that these components are indispensable and replace them with lightweight alternatives. Our 1.3B variant runs at 36 ms per frame, or 28 responses per second (RPS), on a single B200 GPU while matching the generation quality of a state-of-the-art model that is nearly 8x slower. Our 14B variant runs at 45 ms per frame, or 22 RPS, on an 8x B200 GPU node and yields significantly better visual quality and realism. We show that FastFrames enables real-time interaction in applications such as camera-conditioned and physics-conditioned video generation.
comment: Project page: https://apple-aiml-research.github.io/ml-fastframes/
☆ EviSlide-MIL: Multi-Query Pooling and Shared Prediction for Class-Incremental Whole-Slide Image Classification
Zhouhan Qian, Sicheng Chen, Chad Wong, Tianyi Zhang, Enhui Chai, Zeyu Liu, Fei Xia
Histopathological analysis of whole-slide images (WSIs) plays a critical role in cancer diagnosis, and multiple instance learning (MIL) is widely adopted for WSI analysis under weak supervision. As new tumor subtypes are introduced, extending existing MIL models requires learning new classes while retaining knowledge of previously learned ones. This presents a class-incremental learning challenge, where models must acquire new classes with limited access to historical training data and recognize all learned classes without task identifiers at inference. A major obstacle is forgetting, as updates to feature aggregation and prediction modules can degrade performance on previously learned classes. To address this challenge, we propose \textbf{EviSlide-MIL}, a class-incremental WSI framework that integrates multiple learnable queries per class with a shared prediction module. The queries aggregate frozen patch features into class-specific representations, while the shared prediction module limits parameter growth across incremental stages. By freezing queries associated with previously learned classes, EviSlide-MIL preserves their attention patterns for identical inputs, while experience replay and knowledge distillation further mitigate forgetting as shared parameters are updated. Experiments on eight tumor subtypes from The Cancer Genome Atlas demonstrate that EviSlide-MIL achieves improved performance and reduced forgetting compared with competing methods across most learning settings, demonstrating its potential for scalable and knowledge-preserving WSI classification. Code and pretrained models will be released.
☆ Multimodal Masked Diffusion Autoencoder for Modeling Impaired Driving CVPR 2027
John Gideon, Anshul Gupta, Megan Applegate-Kenton, Kayli Battel, Todd J Rowell, Patricio Reyes Gomez, Laporsha Dees, Emily Sumner, Avinash Balachandran, Guy Rosman
Human cognitive state (e.g., distraction, stress), gaze, and behavior interact with the driving environment in subtle ways that AI could use to assist drivers, but ground-truth labels for human cognitive state levels are costly to obtain at scale. We propose a multimodal masked-diffusion autoencoder, ID-MAE, that adds a self-supervised objective to impairment prediction: alongside predicting the impairment label as a masked token, it reconstructs masked gaze and trajectory. To probe the effects of different modalities and types of impairments on model inference, we introduce DIVERT, a driving-simulator dataset containing 103 hours of driving data (n = 109) with ten impairment inductions spanning cognitive, visual, and emotional states, recorded with gaze, vehicle state, and scene video. We demonstrate how ID-MAE affords significant improvements in impairment inference results on both the DIVERT dataset and existing datasets, and enables strong results in additional tasks, such as trajectory and gaze prediction. For location-matched pairs, our model achieves a paired AUC of 0.706 for impairment detection on DIVERT, compared to 0.590 without reconstruction loss, improving over existing baselines. We probe the design space in terms of input modalities, masking scheme, positional encoding, attention mechanism, and decoding. We also investigate the interaction between various impairments in training and inference, demonstrating that visually demanding distractions are separable from cognitive distractions. Code and data will be available upon acceptance.
comment: Equal contribution: John Gideon and Anshul Gupta. 8 pages, 6 figures. Submitted to CVPR 2027
☆ Learning Grounded Reasoning from Human Gaze
Gabriel Sarch, Declan Campbell, Nicholas Budny, Kia Ghods, Katerina Fragkiadaki, Jonathan D. Cohen, Brenden M. Lake, Taylor W. Webb
Human visual reasoning is driven by systematic exploration and extraction of task-relevant visual evidence. Human gaze provides a window into this process, making gaze a useful source of guidance for visually-grounded reasoning in vision-language models (VLMs). However, human gaze also includes noise and redundancies that may transfer poorly to VLMs. In this work, we investigate how human gaze data can be effectively leveraged to improve visual reasoning in VLMs, while maintaining alignment with human behavior. We collect 7,109 human gaze trials from a diverse and challenging set of visual reasoning tasks, and train grounded reasoning models with different forms of gaze guidance. Across evaluations in chart understanding, visual search, and counting, we find that using human gaze as a prior for grounded reasoning consistently outperforms supervision using the full gaze sequence. Based on these findings, we introduce GGR (Gaze-Guided Reasoner), which achieves greater human alignment and more reliable visual grounding while matching or outperforming leading grounded-reasoning baselines in accuracy. Reinforcement learning further improves task accuracy, gaze alignment, and grounding quality despite using no gaze supervision. Behavioral analyses show that gaze supervised models exhibit more visual exploration before arriving at an answer. Our results suggest that the value of human gaze lies in guiding spatial exploration and shaping reasoning behavior without requiring complete imitation of human behavior.
☆ Distortion-Free Semantic Watermarks for Black-Box Generative Models
Aviv Yossef, Or Patashnik, Or Zamir
We present a provably distortion-free semantic watermarking algorithm that requires only black-box sampling access to a generative model and black-box access to a semantic embedding. A watermark is called distortion-free if, averaged over its secret detection key, it leaves the generator's output distribution unchanged; this provides a formal guarantee that watermarking does not reduce output quality. Conventional such watermarks are often brittle to transformations. This is especially problematic for images, where benign operations such as compression, cropping, or resizing change the entire pixel representation. Semantic watermarks therefore require detection to be robust to content-preserving transformations. Previous methods combining these properties rely heavily on specific white-box properties of the underlying model: either to autoregressive text generation or to diffusion-specific access, such as control of the initial noise or diffusion inversion. In contrast, our construction is fully generic: It only interacts with the generative model and the semantic embedding, a function that determines the notion of "preserving content" under which detection should be robust, via sample and query access. We then instantiate this framework for image generation. We characterize the two competing properties required of the semantic embedding: it should remain stable under transformations that preserve an image's content, but should distinguish independent generations from the same prompt. We train an image encoder directly for this tradeoff. The resulting encoder improves separation while maintaining stability over off-the-shelf alternatives and enables strong aggregate detection while remaining robust to various transformations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our watermark scheme on both open-source and closed models, which is possible only due to restriction to black-box access.
comment: Project page: https://avivyossef.github.io/distortion-free-semantic-watermark/ Code: https://github.com/avivyossef/distortion-free-semantic-watermark
☆ Reading Scene States: Uncovering Safety Failures in Vision-Language Models
Tongxi Wu, Yuyang Cheng, Jiacheng Xian, Menglin Yang, Kai Chen, Jian Zhang, Yang Gao
Vision-language models (VLMs) can provide harmful assistance by interpreting visual events, even without an explicit request for the underlying harmful objective. We identify this \textbf{scene-state safety vulnerability} and introduce \textbf{SceneSafetyBench}, comprising 375 image--question pairs spanning Initial, Medium, and Ultimate scene states and five visual presentations. Across eight VLMs, scene-state inputs elicit harmful assistance with attack success rates (ASRs) of 45.6--72.3\%. Comparative analysis across three VLMs shows that scene-state inputs most closely resemble QR-related images in their layer-wise safety-related signal profiles, while exhibiting lower average late-layer readouts and distinct signal dynamics during generation. To turn this vulnerability into a systematic attack, we propose \textbf{S3TA}, which translates harmful objectives into scene states, queries image--question pairs independently, and assembles the responses. On seven MM-SafetyBench categories across eight open-weight and commercial VLMs, S3TA achieves a model-average ASR of \textbf{71.2\%, exceeding the strongest baseline by 6.1 percentage points}. Text-side filters and visual moderation provide limited protection. These findings highlight the need to safeguard the assistance models infer through scene-grounded reasoning, beyond screening input content.
comment: VLM safety, multimodal jailbreaks, and scene-state reasoning
☆ Retrieval-Augmented Correction for Generalist Medical Image Segmentation
Vincenzo Marcianò, Xiaoming Zhang, Michela Antonelli, Sebastien Ourselin, Maria A Zuluaga
Automated segmentation is routinely used as the first step in quantitative image-based clinical workflows, where predicted masks are subsequently reviewed and corrected by human operators. Automated correction of the residual structural errors is currently addressed one anatomy at a time, so the number of trained correctors scales with the number of segmentation targets. We present GRACE, a retrieval-augmented refiner that edits an input mask under context drawn from a shared knowledge base of verified prior cases. The refiner is trained once on a multi-organ corpus spanning compact organs, cavities, branching vessels, and tumour lesions. In the held-out dataset-transfer evaluation, three held-out datasets query a fixed knowledge base built from training data only. A separate leave-one-anatomy-out experiment tests parameter-free index extension: verified cases of an unseen solid organ enter the knowledge base, and the refiner stays frozen. A light shape-aware projection head on a frozen multimodal encoder maps embedding similarity to the shape agreement of the masks, so the knowledge base returns cases that the refiner can use as a shape prior. We evaluate GRACE on 18 public datasets spanning CT, MRI and ultrasound, using nine refinement configurations and seven upstream segmentors that span weak, mid, and strong operating regimes. We report each change with the DSC of its input mask. On the weak tier, the input DSC is 0.386 and GRACE adds up to +0.35 DSC. On a strong segmentor, the input DSC is 0.932 and the mean change is small. Transfer to an imaging modality that is absent from training and from the index is partial and depends on the anatomy, and remains an open research direction. Our results suggest retrieval-conditioned refinement is a practical alternative to anatomy-specific correction models. Code: https://github.com/robustml-eurecom/grace
